nameStory: Wilson's Plover honors Alexander Wilson, a Scottish-American ornithologist often called the 'Father of American Ornithology.' His friend George Ord named this little shorebird after him in 1814, recognizing Wilson's pioneering work in studying and documenting North American birds. It's fitting that this coastal wanderer carries the name of someone who dedicated his life to exploring the continent's avian treasures.
description: Wilson's Plover is a small, chunky shorebird about the size of a robin that lives along sandy beaches and mudflats. These compact birds have relatively large, thick black bills that set them apart from other small plovers. They sport a distinctive black band across their white chest and forehead, with brownish-gray backs that blend perfectly with beach sand. Unlike many shorebirds, they prefer walking and running along the shore rather than wading in deep water.

idTips.label: Thick black bill
idTips.description: The hefty, completely black bill is noticeably thicker and longer than other small plovers - about the width of a thick marker tip and feels substantial if you find a specimen

idTips.label: Black chest band
idTips.description: A bold black stripe runs across the white chest, complete and unbroken in males, sometimes incomplete in females and young birds

idTips.label: Pale legs
idTips.description: Legs range from flesh-colored to pale yellow or gray - never the bright orange or yellow of some other plovers

idTips.label: Sandy brown back
idTips.description: The back and wings are a muted grayish-brown that matches dried beach sand perfectly, with a slightly rough, matte texture to the feathers

idTips.label: White forehead patch
idTips.description: A clean white patch on the forehead is bordered by the black headband, creating a striking contrast that catches sunlight

idTips.label: Chunky build
idTips.description: More robust and stockier than most small shorebirds, with a rounded head and compact body that gives it a sturdy, bulldozer-like appearance

habitat: Wilson's Plovers are extremely rare visitors to New England's sandy beaches, mudflats, and salt marsh edges. When they do appear, look for them on wide, open beaches with shell fragments and wrack lines, particularly around Cape Cod and the islands. They prefer areas where the sand meets muddy or pebbly sections, often near inlet mouths where tidal action creates mixed substrates.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare spring migrants might appear from late April through May on southward-facing beaches. Look for birds in fresh breeding plumage with crisp black markings.
seasonality.summer: Occasional summer visitors in breeding plumage may linger into June or July. Adults show their boldest black chest bands and forehead markings during this season.
seasonality.fall: Most likely season to spot Wilson's Plovers as post-breeding wanderers from August through September. Young birds may show incomplete or brownish chest bands.
seasonality.winter: Very rare in winter, with only exceptional records. Any winter plovers would show duller, brownish plumage instead of the crisp black markings.

funFact: Wilson's Plovers are beach crab specialists that can actually hear crabs moving under the sand - they'll cock their heads, listen intently, then suddenly plunge their thick bills down to snatch hidden fiddler crabs and ghost crabs from their burrows!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the much more common Semipalmated Plover, but Wilson's Plover is noticeably larger with a much thicker, all-black bill (Semipalmated has a thin bill with an orange base). Memory trick: Wilson's bill is 'Hefty' like the trash bags, while Semipalmated's is 'Slim' like a toothpick.
contextualKnowledge: Wilson's Plover is primarily a southern species, making any New England sighting quite exceptional and worth reporting to eBird. The very low observation count of just 12 records reflects how rare this bird is in our region - most New England birders consider it a major find.
compareHints: Among its sand plover relatives, Wilson's Plover is the only one regularly found in the Americas and has the thickest bill of the group. Mountain Plover lives in dry grasslands rather than beaches, while Kentish and Siberian Sand-Plovers are primarily Old World species. Wilson's robust build and specialized crab-hunting bill make it unique among North American plovers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike Wilson's Plover, which loves sandy beaches and has a thick black bill, the Mountain Plover avoids water entirely and has a thinner, all-dark bill.
Compared to Wilson's Plover, the Siberian Sand-Plover is much smaller with a thinner bill and lacks the thick black breast band.
Compared to its closest relative Wilson's Plover, the Kentish Plover is smaller and paler overall, with a thinner, more delicate bill and lighter brown back coloring.
